Field surveys of the Duskytail darter (Etheostoma percnurum) in southern Appalachian streams have provided detailed insights into its life history. Newly emerged prolarvae, having just completed chorion rupture, possess a wet weight at birth of 0.0115 grams [Wwb = 0.0115 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 2.8 millimeters. This minimal initial mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the yolk-sac stage, during which the developing larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. Following the exotrophic transition, the juvenile fish enter a period of rapid somatic growth. Growth trajectory analyses, based on extensive length-at-age data from wild-caught individuals, indicate that the ultimate standard length for this species reaches 5 centimeters [Li = 5 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is modest, consistent with the small body plan typical of many benthic darter species that inhabit shallow, high-gradient riffles.

Reproductive maturation in this species is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age alone, a pattern common among ectothermic vertebrates with indeterminate growth. Mark-recapture studies have demonstrated that individuals attain standard length at puberty when they reach approximately 3.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3.5 centimeters]. This length threshold serves as a reliable proxy for the onset of gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis, with vitellogenesis becoming evident in gravid females during early spring. The consistent relationship between body size and maturity suggests that individuals invest energy first in achieving a sufficient structural framework before allocating resources toward reproduction. This developmental constraint may be particularly important given the energetic demands of the subsequent spawning season, during which females must produce multiple clutches while also maintaining basal metabolic function in thermally variable stream environments.

During the spawning season, which typically extends from late March through early June, females exhibit a remarkable capacity for iteroparous reproduction. At a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is substantial, derived from a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency. Females deposit up to 27 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = up to 27 eggs per clutch] and can produce between 5 and 7 clutches each year [F_R_i = between 5 and 7 clutches each year]. The total annual fecundity at this thermal regime is therefore considerable for a fish of such modest body size. This heightened reproductive output is likely an adaptive response to the high rates of egg mortality characteristic of the species' preferred nesting habitat, where demersal, adhesive eggs are deposited in crevices beneath large cobble and are vulnerable to scouring during spates and predation by crayfish.

The ultimate wet weight of reproductively mature adults provides an additional perspective on the species' energetic scope. Maximum recorded body mass in adults reaches 1.24 grams [Wwi = 1.24 grams], a value estimated from morphometric equations relating standard length to mass using a power function derived from a large sample of field-collected specimens. This asymptotic mass is notably modest, even by darter standards, but is consistent with the species' occupation of a specialized microhabitat within fast-flowing, shallow riffles. The relatively low adult body mass may reflect trade-offs between the energetic costs of maintaining position in high-velocity flow and the resources available for somatic growth and reproduction. Empirical observations suggest that individuals rarely exceed this threshold, indicating that physiological constraints or ecological factors impose a firm upper limit on attainable body size within these populations.

Longevity estimates for the Duskytail darter are based on recapture data from a long-term mark-resight study. The maximum lifespan in the wild has been documented at 730 days [am = 730 days] under ambient stream conditions characterized by a mean annual water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This relatively short life span places the species firmly within an annual-to-biennial life history strategy typical of many small-bodied, short-lived stream fishes. The time since birth at puberty, determined from the same length-at-age data that informed the size-at-maturity estimate, is 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] at 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This one-year maturation window is critical, as it allows spring-spawned individuals to reach sexual maturity by the following spawning season, thereby ensuring that nearly every cohort contributes to the next generation before succumbing to the high overwinter mortality that characterizes these populations.
